turns.question: Is the vegetation at EBTL getting better after restoration started? What about fire—has it gone up or down in the same years?
turns.answer:
Short answer: **vegetation is probably getting better, but the public evidence is still weak; fire does not clearly look lower in the same period.**

What I found:
EBTL says it had started restoration **by October 1, 2022** and that its first three years focused on a native nursery, water-flow learning, planting, invasive removal, and natural regeneration. It also says it has raised **130+ native plant species** and about **15,000 saplings**. That is a good sign that vegetation work is progressing. But I did **not** find a public before/after dataset for EBTL itself, such as yearly canopy cover, NDVI, plant survival, or species richness, so I cannot prove how much the vegetation has improved. Sources: [Nithin Kamath post](https://nithinkamath.me/blog/elephants-by-the-lake.md/), [EBTL About](https://ebtl.earth/about/), [EBTL Restoration Project](https://ebtl.earth/restoration-project/).

For fire, I did **not** find public fire records just for EBTL. The best public proxy I found is **Krishnagiri district** data from Global Forest Watch. That shows **346 VIIRS fire alerts between July 4, 2022 and June 29, 2026**, and says **2023** had the highest tree-cover loss from fire in the district during 2001-2025, with **64 ha** lost that year. So, at least at district scale, fire has **not clearly gone down** during the EBTL restoration years; it was still active and seems to have spiked in 2023. Source: [Global Forest Watch, Krishnagiri dashboard](https://www.globalforestwatch.org/dashboards/country/IND/31/11/?location=WyJjb3VudHJ5IiwiSU5EIiwiMzEiLCIxMSJd&).

What is missing:
EBTL’s exact mapped boundary, yearly vegetation indicators, and an on-site fire log or burned-area record. Without those, the vegetation answer is partly an **estimate**, and the fire answer is only a **regional proxy**, not proof for the EBTL property itself.

turns.question: Which parts of this answer come from satellite data? How detailed is that data?
turns.answer:
Only the **fire proxy** and the **district-level tree-cover-loss-from-fire** part came from satellite-based products.

What came from satellite data:
- **“346 VIIRS fire alerts in Krishnagiri since July 4, 2022”**: this is from **VIIRS active fire alerts** shown by Global Forest Watch, based on NASA satellite detections. These are near-real-time heat/fire detections. Source: [NASA FIRMS active fire data](https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/active_fire/), [GFW fire data explainer](https://www.globalforestwatch.org/blog/data-and-tools/trends-tree-loss-from-fires-unprecedented-detail/).
- **“2023 had the highest tree-cover loss from fire in the district, 64 ha”**: this is from **UMD/GFW tree cover loss from fires**, derived from **Landsat** satellite imagery. Source: [GFW fire-loss explainer](https://www.globalforestwatch.org/blog/data-and-tools/trends-tree-loss-from-fires-unprecedented-detail/), [GFW tree cover loss explainer](https://www.globalforestwatch.org/blog/data-and-tools/2025-tree-cover-loss-data-explained/).

What did **not** come from satellite data:
- The part saying EBTL had restoration activities, native nursery work, saplings, and species counts came from **EBTL’s public pages** and a public blog post, not satellites. Sources: [EBTL About](https://ebtl.earth/about/), [EBTL Restoration Project](https://ebtl.earth/restoration-project/), [Nithin Kamath post](https://nithinkamath.me/blog/elephants-by-the-lake.md/).

How detailed the satellite data is:
- **VIIRS fire alerts**: about **375 m** pixels. Good for seeing that a fire/heat signal was detected nearby, but **not good for drawing exact burned boundaries** or proving what happened on one small site. Source: [NASA FIRMS](https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/active_fire/).
- **Tree cover loss from fires**: about **30 m** pixels from Landsat, updated **yearly**. This is much finer, but it mainly captures **stand-replacing canopy loss**. It can miss **low-intensity understory fires** that do not remove canopy clearly enough at 30 m. Source: [GFW fire-loss explainer](https://www.globalforestwatch.org/blog/data-and-tools/trends-tree-loss-from-fires-unprecedented-detail/).

What is missing:
- I did **not** find a public **EBTL boundary file** or an **EBTL-specific satellite analysis**.
- So the satellite part of the earlier answer is **district-scale**, not a direct measurement of the EBTL property itself.

turns.question: Can we say the restoration work caused these changes, or not?
turns.answer:
Short answer: **no, not from the public evidence we have.**

What we can say:
- **Found:** EBTL started restoration by **October 1, 2022** and has done planting, nursery work, invasive removal, and regeneration support. Sources: [EBTL About](https://ebtl.earth/about/), [EBTL Restoration Project](https://ebtl.earth/restoration-project/), [Nithin Kamath post](https://nithinkamath.me/blog/elephants-by-the-lake.md/).
- **Found:** At the **district** level, public satellite data shows fire activity continued during these years, and **2023** had high tree-cover loss from fire in Krishnagiri. Source: [Global Forest Watch, Krishnagiri](https://www.globalforestwatch.org/dashboards/country/IND/31/11/?location=WyJjb3VudHJ5IiwiSU5EIiwiMzEiLCIxMSJd&).

What we **cannot** say:
- **We cannot say restoration caused vegetation improvement.**
- **We cannot say restoration caused fire to go up or down.**

Why not:
- The public data I found is **not site-specific enough** for EBTL.
- I did **not** find a public **before/after vegetation dataset** for the EBTL property.
- I did **not** find a public **EBTL fire history** for the same years.
- I did **not** find a **comparison area** or a method that separates restoration effects from weather, regional fire patterns, grazing, or other factors.

Best careful wording:
- **Found:** “Vegetation work is clearly happening at EBTL.”
- **Estimate:** “Vegetation may be improving.”
- **Not supported yet:** “Restoration caused the improvement” or “restoration caused fire to decrease/increase.”

What is missing to make a causal claim:
- A mapped EBTL boundary.
- Site-level yearly vegetation measures, before and after restoration.
- Site-level fire or burned-area records for the same years.
- Ideally, a comparison with similar nearby untreated land.
